issues.issue: Four separate lessors are each recited as "acting in his/her sole and separate interest," which does not say whether each leases only an undivided share or whether they jointly lease the whole tract. Read with Paragraph 9's lesser-interest clause, the extent of what each Chambers lessor conveyed is left open.

The grant of the right to "transport by pipelines or otherwise across and through said lands oil, gas and their constituents from the subject and other lands," surviving the lease term, cannot be squared with Paragraph 25 and Addendum ¶20, which deny Lessee any right to move gas from other lands across the premises. Which controls is sharpened by the Addendum priority clause.

The premises are described both by enumerated tax parcels with stated acreages and by a catch-all covering "all the property owned by Lessor or to which the Lessor may have any rights," "containing 904.10 acres, more or less," a figure the listed parcels do not add up to. Whether the specific parcels or the general Mother Hubbard words bound the leasehold is a general-versus-specific question.

The habendum extends the term so long as gas is "produced or are capable of being produced on the premises in paying quantities, in the judgment of the Lessee"; "capable of being produced" and "paying quantities" are undefined and the measure is committed to Lessee's own judgment. Whether the lease survives without actual marketed production turns on that phrase.

The term is extended "as provided in Paragraph 7 following," but Paragraph 7 addresses only the adequacy of consideration and Lessee's right to drill or not drill and says nothing about maintaining the term; the shut-in mechanism is in Paragraph 6. The cross-reference cannot be given effect as written.

This paragraph deems a well "commenced when preparations for drilling have been commenced," while Addendum ¶16 defines commencement of operations as entry with equipment to build access roads followed by a drilling rig for spudding. The two definitions cannot both govern, and the Addendum priority clause makes the choice consequential.

Lessee may elect to pay "the market price for such one-eighth royalty oil at the published rate for oil of like grade and gravity," without identifying the publication, market or point of valuation. "Market price" and "published rate" have no benchmark in the instrument.

The clause fixes gas royalty at one-eighth of "the price paid to Lessee," and the post-production-cost deduction language that followed is struck through, leaving it unresolved whether royalty is net or gross of gathering, compression, dehydration and transportation. "The price paid to Lessee" is itself undefined for sales to affiliates.

This subparagraph lets Lessee deduct from royalty "Lessor's share of any severance or other tax imposed by any government body," which cannot be squared with Addendum ¶14 making Lessee responsible for any increase in property taxes levied on Lessor because of Lessee's operations. The Addendum priority clause puts the two squarely against each other.

The payee line is not filled in — payment is to be "made payable to the order of and mailed to: ABOVE ADDRESS" — so "the said named person" who is to continue as Lessor's agent has no antecedent. With four lessors at four different addresses, who is to be paid and where is unstated.

Paragraph 6 provides a shut-in royalty but never says that paying it keeps the lease in force, which must be read against Paragraph 2's habendum extending the term while gas is "capable of being produced." Whether shut-in payments hold the lease past the primary term is unresolved between the two.

Paragraph 2 continues the term "as provided in Paragraph 7 following," yet this paragraph supplies only an acknowledgment of consideration and a right to drill or not drill. Read together, Paragraph 7 cannot perform the function Paragraph 2 assigns it.

Pooling is capped at 640 acres "or such larger unit as may be required by state law or regulation," a trigger with no applicable boundary in Pennsylvania, and the same sentence requires Lessee to "maintain a well density of at least 1 well per 160 acres contained in such well." The size limit and the density obligation are both indeterminate as written.

Paragraph 9 directs that royalties be divided among several owners in proportion to acreage owned of the entire leased acreage, while Paragraph 8 allocates royalty on the acreage consolidated into a development unit. Which allocation governs a pooled tract owned by several persons is left to be reconciled.

No change in Lessor's ownership binds Lessee until it is furnished "certified copies of all recorded instruments or documents and other information necessary to establish a complete chain of record title," leaving Lessee to judge what is "necessary" and what a "complete" chain requires. The standard for effective notice is undefined.

"Lessor agrees that when and if the within lease is assigned, the Lessee herein shall have no further obligations hereunder" does not say whether liabilities already accrued, or continuing covenants, are released along with future ones. The scope of the release on assignment is the defect.

This paragraph has Lessor waive "notice of any assignment or transfer of the within lease," which cannot be squared with Addendum ¶17 requiring Lessee to give Lessor written notice of any assignment of 51% or more within fourteen days. The Addendum priority clause makes the conflict live.

The paragraph sends "any damages if not mutually agreed upon" to three disinterested appraisers and then adds "Arbitration shall be mandatory," without saying whether that sentence covers only damage valuation or every dispute under the lease. Whether this is an appraisal clause or an arbitration agreement is the ambiguity.

Lessor must "abide by all reasonable safety policies of Lessee," a body of policies made unilaterally by Lessee and nowhere identified, with "reasonable" left unmeasured. The setback examples are introduced as "including but not limited to," so the obligation's outer limit is unstated.

Surrender is declared "a cancellation of all liabilities under the same of each and all parties hereto" as to the surrendered premises, which cannot be squared with Addendum ¶¶1–2 imposing repair and restoration duties that by their terms follow the cessation of operations. Whether surrender wipes out accrued restoration obligations is the conflict.

The clause reduces "the land rental hereinbefore set forth" in proportion to acreage surrendered, but Paragraph 3 states this is a paid-up lease and no land rental is set forth anywhere. The reduction mechanism has no antecedent to operate on.

The clause says that "in no event shall the within lease expire for a period of ninety (90) days after the termination of any force majeure," wording that on its face postpones expiration rather than extending the term, and the triggering events are an open-ended "including but not limited to" list. What counts as force majeure and how long it tolls the term are both left uncertain.

Notice is made "precedent to the bringing of any action by Lessor on said lease for any cause," and Lessee need only "meet or commence to meet all or any part of the breaches" within thirty days. Whether the notice requirement bars all claims and what suffices to "commence to meet" a breach are undefined.

Lessor promises to grant "no other lease for the minerals covered by this lease," which sits against Addendum ¶21 stating that Lessee has not acquired coalbed methane rights without Lessor's prior written consent. Whether Lessor may lease coalbed methane to another turns on reading the two together.

The warranty that there are no "commercially producing wells currently existing" on or within a unit including the premises leaves "commercially producing" undefined. What quantity or profitability makes a well commercially producing is not fixed anywhere in the lease.

The length of the additional primary term is left blank — "one additional primary term of ____ commencing on the date that the lease would have expired" — so the duration of any extension is not stated. The option also fixes no deadline by which Lessee must exercise it.

The provision declares that "no implied covenant, agreement or obligation shall be read into this agreement," which must be reconciled with Paragraph 4(B)'s royalty measured on "the price paid to Lessee," a measure that presupposes a duty to market. Whether the disclaimer defeats implied marketing and development covenants is the question.

Paragraph 21 covers Clean and Green assessments caused by Lessee's operations, while Addendum ¶13 covers the same ground and adds the Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program. The two overlapping promises differ in scope, and the Addendum priority clause requires a court to decide which governs.

Lessee indemnifies Lessor against all claims arising out of its operations "unless such damage or injury is caused solely by Lessor's acts, omissions, or negligence," which by negative implication covers losses to which Lessor's negligence merely contributed. Whether the clause indemnifies Lessor against Lessor's own negligence is not expressed.

Paragraph 23 requires well, road and pipeline locations to be fixed "by mutual consent between Lessor and Lessee," while Addendum ¶3 substitutes a written approval form with deemed approval if Lessor does not respond in thirty days. Mutual consent and deemed consent cannot both control the same decision.

Thirty days' notice is given "to allow the Lessor to harvest any marketable timber, or domesticated crops," without defining "marketable" or saying what happens if thirty days is not enough to harvest. The extent of Lessor's harvesting right is left vague.

This paragraph bars Lessee from asserting the right to transport gas from other lands across the premises, which cannot be squared with the Paragraph 1 grant of exactly that right, expressly surviving the lease term. One of the two must yield.

The restriction is phrased as an agreement "not to assert the right" rather than a denial of the right, and it lapses "unless the lands covered by this lease are pooled, communitized, or included in a production unit." Whether pooling any part of the tract lifts the restriction entirely is unstated.

This paragraph makes the Addendum part of the lease, while Paragraph 20 declares that the instrument contains all agreements of the parties and admits no implied obligation. Read together with the Addendum's own priority clause, the relationship between the two documents must be worked out.

The priority clause makes the Addendum prevail over "the inconsistent provisions of the main body," but it does not identify which provisions are inconsistent, and it operates against Paragraph 20's integration clause. Deciding whether Paragraph 1's transport and storage grants are "inconsistent" with Addendum ¶¶8 and 20 is exactly what it leaves to be construed.

Addendum ¶1 requires restoration "as nearly as possible" to the condition existing at the commencement of drilling, within 90 days "weather permitting," while Addendum ¶2 requires restoration "to as near its original condition as is reasonably possible" with no deadline. Two different standards and baselines govern the same obligation.

Addendum ¶2 measures restoration against the land's "original condition" and imposes no time limit, while Addendum ¶1 measures it against the condition at commencement of drilling and requires completion within 90 days. The two cannot both be the operative standard.

Addendum ¶3's written-form procedure, under which Lessor's silence for thirty days "shall constitute Lessor's approval," cannot be squared with Paragraph 23's requirement that locations be fixed by mutual consent. It also obliges Lessor to supply an alternate location Lessee "deems to be economically feasible," a standard set by Lessee alone.

Addendum ¶4 forbids Lessee to take water from Lessor's ponds, springs or creeks without written consent, while Paragraph 14 gives Lessee the privilege of using sufficient water for operating on the premises. The two provisions cannot both be given full effect.

Addendum ¶5 requires all pipeline laid by Lessee to be buried at least 32 inches, while Paragraph 12 requires burial only "when so requested by the Lessor." Whether burial is automatic or on request is left to be reconciled.

The paragraph caps access roads at 40 feet "during actual drilling operation" and 16 feet for a producing well, without saying which limit applies between drilling and production or after a dry hole. Restoration is owed only "as close as is practicable," an unmeasured standard.

Addendum ¶8 states that Lessee has not acquired rights to drill an underground gas or oil storage well, while Paragraph 1 grants the right of "injecting and storing, air, gas, brine and other substances from any source and into any subsurface strata." The storage grant and the storage denial are in direct conflict.

Addendum ¶9 fixes crop damages at "the current value in the area" of the crop being cultivated, while Paragraph 12 sends damages to growing crops to a three-appraiser determination. Which mechanism values crop damage is unresolved.

Addendum ¶10 bars mechanics' liens from reaching the landowners' royalty interest, while Paragraph 11 gives Lessee the right to pay any lien against Lessor's interest, become subrogated, and direct royalties to satisfying existing liens. The protection and the royalty-diversion right pull against each other.

The water-replacement duty is triggered by a "material adverse change in the quality of Lessor's water supply," a term left undefined, and only if experienced "during or immediately after the completion of Lessee's drilling operations." Both the threshold and the window are indeterminate.

Addendum ¶12 provides the same three-appraiser procedure for damages as Paragraph 12 but omits the sentence "Arbitration shall be mandatory." Whether the Addendum displaces mandatory arbitration for timber and improvement damages is left open by the priority clause.

The paragraph ends by promising to pay the additional cost, taxes, penalties and fines "so levied against the Lessee," although the entire clause concerns assessments levied against the Lessor. The mistaken word makes the operative promise circular.

Addendum ¶16 defines commencement of operations as entry with equipment to build access roads followed by a drilling rig for spudding, while Paragraph 3 deems a well commenced "when preparations for drilling have been commenced." The two definitions cannot both govern when operations begin.

Addendum ¶17 requires Lessee to give Lessor written notice of any assignment of 51% or greater interest within fourteen days, while Paragraph 11 has Lessor waive notice of any assignment. The waiver and the notice duty are in direct conflict.

The location fee is payable "upon commencement of drilling operations on the leased premises" without saying whether it is owed once or for each well drilled. The stated amount is also rendered inconsistently in words and figures.

The audit right runs only "for the purpose of determining the quantity of said gas and/or oil produced, metered and sold," so it does not on its face reach price or the deductions that determine royalty under Paragraph 4(B). The scope of what may be audited is the defect.

Addendum ¶20 denies Lessee the right "to transport foreign gas across the premises described in this lease," which cannot be squared with Paragraph 1's express grant of the right to transport oil and gas from other lands across the leasehold, surviving the term. This is the sharpest conflict in the instrument.

"Foreign gas" is undefined, and the permitted transport extends to gas "produced from the premises described" and from "the premises unitized herewith," leaving unclear how gas from a pooled unit is characterized. What is foreign and what is unitized is the ambiguity.

Addendum ¶21 states that Lessee has not acquired the right to develop or produce coalbed methane gas without Lessor's prior written consent, while Paragraphs 1, 2, 4 and 8 lease coalbed methane gas, measure royalty on it and hold the lease by its production. The grant and the reservation cannot both be given effect.
